title: The gourd in the tree
translation: Live simply, don't show off, don't hoard money, don't grab at things. That's the way to be. Wise people have hardly ever been rich.

Xu You, back in ancient China, owned nothing at all and drank water out of his cupped hands. Someone saw that and gave him a gourd to drink from. One day he hung it on a branch, the wind made it rattle, and he threw it away because of the noise. Then he went back to drinking from his hands. Imagine how light that must have felt.
Sun Chen had no blanket in winter, just a bundle of straw. He slept on it at night and put it away in the morning.
The Chinese thought these things were wonderful, which is why they wrote them down and passed them on. People here wouldn't even bother to tell the story.

literal: That a person keep himself frugal, put away luxury, not have wealth, and not be greedy for the world: that would surely be splendid.
From of old, it is rare for wise people to be rich.

In China, a man called Xu You had no stores at all to his name and drank water by scooping it up in his hands; someone who saw this gave him a thing called a gourd, and when he once hung it on a tree branch, it rattled when blown by the wind, and saying it was noisy, he threw it away.
And again he drank water by cupping it in his hands.
How refreshed his heart must have been.
Sun Chen had no bedding in the winter months, and had one bundle of straw, on which he lay at night and which he put away in the morning.
It is because the Chinese thought these things splendid that they recorded them and passed them on to the world.
The people (of our land) would not even pass these on in stories.

notes.text: つづまやか: 'frugal, compact, kept small'. The whole first sentence is one ideal with four parts; the translation turns it into four short pieces of advice.
Xu You, a legendary hermit of ancient China. In the best-known story about him, the ruler Yao offered him the empire, and he went and washed his ears in a river because he had heard such a thing.
A dried gourd, used as a cup or a bottle.

Sun Chen, a poor scholar of the Han dynasty. Both stories, Xu You's gourd and Sun Chen's straw, appear in the Mengqiu, a Chinese primer of famous anecdotes that every educated Japanese reader had learned.

notes.quote: いかばかり心の中すずしかりけむ
notes.text: すずし: 'cool, refreshed, free'. けむ: a guess about the past, 'must have been'.

notes.quote: これらの人は語りも伝ふべからず
notes.text: これらの{人|ひと} is usually understood as 'the people of this country'. The Chinese made these men into examples; in Japan nobody would think such poverty worth a story. The section ends on that dry contrast.
